title: Kinematics in One Dimension
summary: Motion along a line is described by position, velocity, and acceleration. Velocity is $v=dx/dt$ and acceleration $a=dv/dt$. For constant acceleration, the kinematic equations relate displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.

average vs instantaneous.plain: Over an interval vs at an instant.

concept_sections.heading: Position, velocity, acceleration
concept_sections.explanation: Velocity is the derivative of position, $v=dx/dt$; acceleration is the derivative of velocity, $a=dv/dt$. On graphs, slope of $x(t)$ is $v$, slope of $v(t)$ is $a$.

concept_sections.heading: The kinematic equations
concept_sections.explanation: For constant $a$: $v=v_0+at$, $x=x_0+v_0t+\tfrac12at^2$, and $v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta x$. Pick the equation missing the variable you don't have.
math_steps: Choose the equation without the extra variable.

concept_sections.heading: Free fall
concept_sections.explanation: Near Earth, gravity gives constant downward acceleration $g\approx9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. The same kinematic equations apply with $a=-g$.

concept_sections.heading: Graphical analysis
concept_sections.explanation: Slopes give rates (position→velocity→acceleration); areas give accumulations (area under $v(t)$ is displacement).

concept_sections.heading: Average vs instantaneous
concept_sections.explanation: Average velocity is total displacement over total time; instantaneous velocity is the limit as the interval shrinks — the derivative.

real_world_examples.title: Braking distance
real_world_examples.scenario: A car brakes to a stop.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: $v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta x$ finds the stopping distance from speed and deceleration.

real_world_examples.title: Dropping a ball off a cliff
real_world_examples.scenario: A stone falls from a height.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Free-fall kinematics with $a=-g$ gives the fall time and impact speed.

A ball thrown up at $20$ m/s reaches what maximum height?
